My plan isn't syncing across devices
Choose a folder your cloud provider (iCloud Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, …) actually syncs — a folder that only exists on this computer stays local. Milestone rereads the file every 45s and on every save and merges changes, so two devices editing at once won't lose work; and because it can see the whole folder it also merges the “conflicted copies” a sync service makes when two devices save at the same moment. Chrome does not allow Desktop, Documents or Downloads themselves — pick a folder inside them.

How this works

Durations, lags and dependencies count working days only — weekdays that work and are not a holiday. Auto Scheduled tasks start and finish on working days; Manually Scheduled tasks keep the dates you give them. Days off are shaded in the Gantt chart. Public-holiday presets are a starting point — check them against your own calendar; regional and company days differ. Dates already in the plan are not moved when you change this, and other plans keep their own calendar.

Changes apply when you save.

Advanced

On (the standard): a constraint date overrides what the task's links say. Off: the links win, and the constraint shows as unmet (warning icon) without forcing the date.

Level resources

Delays a task that asks for more of a resource than it has, to the next span where every resource it's assigned to has room — never earlier than its own dependencies already allow.

Never pushes the project's own finish out — a conflict that can't be resolved this way is left in place and listed below.

Help

Building a plan
Finding your way: the top bar is the same everywhere — your plan, the views (Tasks · Gantt for the schedule, Resource Plan · Resources for the people — Resources lists the people: rates, days off), Schedule (baselines, rescheduling, levelling), Data, and the gear for the plan's settings (calendar, precision, rules, currency, custom fields). The toolbar below changes with the view and shows what that view needs; on a narrow window the rest is under More.
The status bar along the bottom shows how new tasks are scheduled (click to change), how many tasks there are and are selected, the active filters, and — in the Gantt and Resource Plan — a zoom slider. The Task Form switch is its first button.
Add Task inserts a task below the selected one, or at the bottom when nothing is selected. Each task has a start and end date and a % complete, and can be a milestone (a one-day diamond).
Dates and times in dialogs are typed in the format of the list — 24.12.2026 (or 24.12.26, 24.12.), 14:30 (or 1430, 2:30pm) — or picked with the calendar button. Something unreadable is refused, marks the box red and puts the old value back; Enter settles a box, and in a single-purpose dialog like Reschedule or Baselines it applies the dialog.
Date format: Plan settings → Formats chooses how dates (dd.mm.yyyy, dd/mm/yyyy, mm/dd/yyyy, yyyy-mm-dd) and times (24-hour or 12-hour AM / PM) are shown and typed on this computer — click a tile, or Use my browser's format. The plan itself isn't changed, and the list, dialogs, Gantt, Print, Excel and CSV all follow it. A date typed in the other order is still understood when it can only mean one thing.
Right-click a task (in the list, or its row in the chart) for a menu with Edit, Add task, Add empty line, Duplicate, Copy, Cut, Paste, Indent, Outdent and Delete. Right-clicking on the empty part of the list offers Add task, Add empty line and Paste. The buttons for the selected tasks (Edit, Duplicate, Copy, Delete) appear in the toolbar while something is selected; with one task Edit opens the same dialog as a double-click.
Row colour (in the task dialog, or under Edit for several tasks) marks a task in the list with a stripe at its left edge and a light tint of the same colour — also behind its bar in the Gantt chart, and in the printout and the Excel export. The bars themselves keep their status colours: green complete, red late, blue in progress, grey not started.
Add empty line (in the menu next to Add Task, or on the right-click menu) inserts a blank row below the selected task (below its whole block when it is a group) to separate blocks of tasks. It has an ID but no name, dates or WBS, is never scheduled, charted or linked, and can be moved, indented, copied and deleted like any row.
Indent and Outdent build the work breakdown structure. A parent task's own dates and progress roll up from its sub-tasks, and its WBS code (such as 2.1.3) follows the outline.
Drag a task's line up or down to reorder it — a parent brings its sub-tasks along.
Duplicate (on a task's line, in the toolbar once a task is selected, or on the right-click menu) makes an exact copy right below it, including all its sub-tasks and their sub-tasks. Undo takes it back.
Mark complete on the right-click menu sets the selected tasks to 100% in one click (groups and finished tasks are skipped). Undo takes it back.
The double arrow above the ID numbers steps through the outline: collapse every group, then open the first level, then the next level, and so on until everything is open — then it starts over.
Selecting several tasks
Ctrl/Cmd+click adds a task to the selection or takes it out; Shift+click selects every visible row from the last one you clicked; Ctrl/Cmd+A selects all visible tasks; Esc (or the “N selected” chip in the toolbar) clears it.
Indent, Outdent, Duplicate, Copy and Delete then act on all of them (a group brings its sub-tasks). The Edit button in the toolbar opens the full task dialog for one selected task (the same as a double-click) and, with several selected, Edit tasks: tick the fields to change — % complete, Resource, Task Mode, Row colour, Move dates by a number of working days, Add predecessor, and any custom field you show — and Apply (or Enter). It is one Undo step.
Copy and paste
Ctrl/Cmd+C (or the copy button) copies the selected tasks with their sub-tasks and the links between them; Ctrl/Cmd+V pastes them below the selected task at its level — into this plan or another. Ctrl/Cmd+X cuts.
The same copy is a table Excel understands: a header row, the ID column and the columns you show, names indented by level.
It works the other way too: copy rows in Excel — with a header such as Task Name, Start, Finish, Duration, % Complete, Resource, Predecessors — and paste them here. Indented names or a WBS / Outline Level column give the outline; dates like 07.09.2026, durations like 5 days and links like 3FS+2 are read, and “TBD” dates make a Manually Scheduled task.
Find a task
Press ? anywhere (or use Keyboard shortcuts at the top of this window) for the list of keyboard shortcuts.
Ctrl/Cmd+K, / or the Find button opens a search: part of a name or a note (every word must match), a WBS code such as 2.1, #12 for the task with that ID, or @anna for a resource, and status:late for the late tasks (also complete, future, on for on schedule — combine it with words). Enter goes to the task — folded groups open, a filter that would hide it steps aside, the row (and in the Gantt view the bar) scrolls into view and flashes. Shift+Enter shows only the matches.
Find and replace (Ctrl+H, or the link in the Find window) changes text in one field of many tasks at once — Task Name, Resource, Notes or a custom text field — for all tasks, the filtered ones or the selected ones. The preview shows every change first; one Undo takes it all back.
Undo and redo
The two round arrows at the left of the toolbar take back and repeat your changes one step at a time — an edit together with everything it moved in the schedule, an added or deleted task, a baseline, a change of the working calendar. The toast says what was undone and offers the opposite step.
The history is kept in memory only: it starts empty when you open the app or switch to another plan, and it is cleared when changes from another device are merged in — so undo can never take back somebody else's work.
Keyboard
Ctrl/Cmd+ZUndo Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+Z or Ctrl+YRedo EnterSave the cell you are editing EscCancel an edit, close a dialog or menu, or clear the selection Ctrl/Cmd+ASelect all visible tasks Ctrl/Cmd+C X VCopy, cut and paste tasks (or rows from Excel) DeleteDelete the selected tasks (after asking) Ctrl/Cmd+K or /Find a task Ctrl/Cmd+PPrint or save as PDF
In a text field Ctrl/Cmd+Z is the browser's own undo for what you are typing; with a dialog open it leaves the plan alone.
Task Mode
Auto Scheduled (chart icon) tasks follow their predecessors and constraints.
Manually Scheduled (pushpin) tasks stay exactly where you put them: predecessors never move them, their Start, Finish (a manual milestone's too) and Duration can be free text such as “TBD”, and a warning triangle appears if one starts earlier than its predecessors allow. They are drawn with a dashed bar and left out of the critical path.
Click the icon in the Task Mode column (or use the Task Mode field in a task's dialog) to switch. Switching to Auto moves the task to the earliest date its links allow. New tasks are in the menu next to Add Task sets the mode a newly added task gets — Auto Scheduled by default.
Task Type and Work
Each task has a Task Type — Fixed Units (default), Fixed Duration or Fixed Work — and a Work figure (e.g. 4h, 2d), both set in the task's dialog or as grid columns. Editing Duration, Work or a resource recalculates whichever of the other two the type says is not fixed, keeping Work = Duration × the assigned resources' total percentage.
Fixed Units and Fixed Work with Effort-driven ticked (a checkbox beside Task Type, off by default): adding a second resource shortens the Duration — two people finish faster. Unticked, the resource just adds Work and nothing moves. Fixed Duration always grows the Work instead and the schedule stays put.
Dependencies
Open a task and add a predecessor to link it to another task: Finish-to-Start, Start-to-Start, Finish-to-Finish or Start-to-Finish. In the list you can type them directly, the way MS Project writes them: 3, 3FS, 3SS+2d, 4FF-1w, several separated by , or ;.
Lag and lead: a positive number delays the dependent task, a negative number lets it overlap and start early. 3FS+2 waits 2 extra days after task 3 finishes; 3FS-2 starts 2 days before task 3 finishes. Units are days (d), weeks (w) or hours (h), counted in working time by default; an e prefix (3FS+2ed, 2ew, 2eh) makes it elapsed — real calendar time, crossing weekends and holidays without skipping them, as in MS Project. Percentage lags are not supported.
A circular dependency is flagged with a warning icon and stops auto-scheduling for the tasks involved.
Automatic scheduling, as in MS Project
An Auto task always sits at the earliest date its links allow. Move a predecessor later and the dependent tasks are pushed later; make it shorter, finish it early (record an Actual Finish) or delete it, and they are pulled earlier.
A date you choose is kept. Type a Start later than its links allow (or drag the bar later, or change it in the task's dialog) — a deliberate delay — and the task stays there with a Start No Earlier Than constraint at that date; a later Finish gets Finish No Earlier Than. Links can still push the task later, but never pull it before that date.
A date that is not a delay adds no constraint: a milestone or a task with no links stays a plain as-soon-as-possible task. Change or remove a constraint in the task's dialog. Manual tasks and tasks that have already started are never moved.
Tasks always honor their constraint dates (Schedule → Plan settings → Scheduling rules → Advanced) is on by default: a constraint always wins over what a task's links would otherwise compute. Turn it off and a link wins instead when the two disagree — the constraint still shows as unmet (the warning icon), it just no longer forces the date.
Working calendar
Each plan has its own working days — Monday to Friday unless you change it (Schedule → Plan settings… → Calendar). Durations, lags and dependencies count working days only: a 5-day task that starts on a Monday finishes on that Friday, and its successor starts the next Monday.
Add holidays and other days off in the same dialog: a single day (just the First day), a longer break (add a Last day), or a day that comes back every year, each with an optional name — the Add button says how many days it adds. They count as days off exactly like weekends, and are shaded in the Gantt chart.
Public holidays: pick a country or region (Germany with each of its states, Austria, Switzerland, the UK, Ireland, the US, Canada, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Spain, Italy) and the years, then Add public holidays. Movable ones (Easter, Ascension, Thanksgiving …) are worked out for each year; days that fall on a day off anyway are left out.
Treat the presets as a starting point: check them against your own calendar — regional and company days differ — and edit or remove any entry.
Auto tasks start and finish on working days — a date you type or drag to on a day off moves to the nearest working day. Manual tasks keep exactly the dates you give them. Changing the calendar or the holidays never moves dates that are already in the plan.
Actual dates and status
Actual Start and Actual Finish record what really happened, and they are the schedule: an Actual Start becomes the task's Start (a running task keeps its duration, so its Finish moves with it) and an Actual Finish becomes its Finish. The tasks that depend on it are re-planned from those dates — later or earlier.
Click the % cell of a task to type its % complete (0–100; 50 or 50%). A group's % is worked out from its sub-tasks, so it is not editable.
Recording an Actual Finish marks the task 100% complete and fills an empty Actual Start. A task that has started or finished is not rescheduled any more; a warning triangle appears if its predecessors say it couldn't have started yet.
A group shows the actual dates of the tasks in it: the earliest actual start, and an actual finish once everything in it has finished.
Remaining Duration (the duration still to go, from % complete) and Status (Complete, On Schedule, Late or Future Task, judged against today) are worked out for you.
Baselines and variance
The bar is the current schedule. To keep the original plan, set a baseline (Schedule menu → Baseline…): a frozen copy of every task's Start and Finish, only ever taken when you ask. Keep up to eleven — Baseline and Baseline 1–10 — and choose which one to compare with.
The baseline shows as a thin grey line under each bar in the Gantt chart (the Baseline button in the Gantt toolbar hides it).
The Start Variance, Finish Variance, Baseline Start/Finish/Duration and Duration Variance columns show how far each task has moved, in working days (working minutes for a leaf task in an hours & minutes plan) — positive means later than the baseline.
Reschedule remaining work… (Schedule menu) catches the plan up with a status date you choose: an overdue task moves there, an in-progress task keeps its remaining work from that date if it would otherwise finish later. Finished tasks and tasks ahead of schedule are left alone. The dialog says how many would move, with a Which tasks list; in an hours & minutes plan the status date has a time. Undo brings everything back.
Hours & minutes planning
A plan counts whole days by default. Switch it to Hours & minutes when tasks last hours rather than days — a setting of that plan alone, so your other plans stay in days. Times of day then appear everywhere: the list, the dialogs, the chart, Remaining and baselines, Excel, MS Project XML and print.
Scheduling precision (Schedule → Plan settings… → Calendar → Days or hours): the standard is whole days, but a plan can switch to Hours & minutes so tasks can start and finish at a time of day. Set the working day's start/end and its breaks there too; date fields, Duration and the columns adapt once it's on. Switching in keeps a task's whole day; switching back drops every time and warns first if that would lose something.
Different hours on some days (Plan settings → Calendar → Days or hours): add a weekday — a short Friday, say — and give it its own start, end and breaks. A task with no time of its own then starts and finishes at its day's own open and close, and the chart, print-out, Excel and MS Project export follow each day's hours.
Lags are working time in an hours & minutes plan: type 3FS+2h, 5SS-30m or 1FS+1d in the Predecessors cell (d is a working day, w five of them; a bare number is hours), or the same in the task dialog and Edit tasks. Switching a plan to Hours & minutes converts its lags (2 days become 16 hours).
In an hours & minutes plan the chart gets an Hours scale (20 px an hour, the day over its 24 hours; nights, the lunch break and days off are shaded). Drag a bar, or its edges, in 15-minute steps: an Auto task lands on working time (a move into the lunch break comes out after it), a Manual task goes exactly where you drop it, and linked tasks follow.
In the list, click a Start, Finish or Actual cell and type date and time (07.09.2026 14:30) — a date alone keeps the time, a time alone (14:30) keeps the date. The Duration cell takes 4h, 90m, 2d or 1w. The Excel Gantt sheet gets one column per working hour.
Paste and CSV import read a time after a date (07.09.2026 14:30, also 2:30 PM), durations like 2.5 hrs or 90 min, and minute lags — and copying rows keeps them. A custom Date column takes a time too, and Print / PDF shows the times and can use an Hours scale.
Task Form
Task Form (the toggle at the left of the status bar, Tasks and Gantt views) opens a pane below the list with the selected task's details, as in MS Project: name, duration, start, finish, Task Type, % complete, Effort driven, Manually Scheduled, and tables of its resources (Units, Work) and predecessors (Type, Lag). Drag its top edge to resize.
Change several fields, then OK (or Enter) applies them together — one Undo step; Cancel (or Esc) throws them away. Previous / Next apply first, then move on. Until you click OK or Cancel the form stays on its task, even if you select another row.
Notes, deadlines and slack
Notes: the task dialog's Notes tab. A task with notes shows a note icon by its name — point at it to read them, click to edit. There is also a Notes column.
A Deadline (task dialog, or the Deadline column) is a target date: it never moves the task. When the task finishes later, the deadline turns red, a flag appears by the name, and the chart's arrow on that day turns red (green while it's kept).
Total Slack (a column) is how far a task can slip without moving the plan's finish — 0 on the critical path, red when negative. A group shows the least of its tasks.
Sorting
Sort by any column from the top of its filter panel (the funnel), or right-click its header. Each group's tasks are sorted, the outline stays, and task numbers don't change. The status bar says Sorted by … — its × goes back to the plan's order. While sorted, tasks can't be dragged or indented.
Group (toolbar, Tasks view) gathers the tasks under a header per value of a column: Status, Resource, Task Mode, Task Type, a month of Start / Finish / Deadline, % Complete in bands or a custom field. Click a header to fold its group; it shows the count, span, % and cost of its tasks.
While grouped, only tasks without sub-tasks are listed and moving or indenting is off; the Gantt view keeps the outline. Right-click a column header for Group by …. Nothing in the plan changes.
Columns
Click Columns in the toolbar to tick the columns you want and reorder them. The Tasks view and the Gantt view each remember their own set on this device; Task Name always stays.
Add task under the last row (Tasks view) adds a task at the end of the plan; the toolbar's Add Task adds it below the selected one. The Resource Sheet ends with Add resource.
Use the keyboard in the list: the arrow keys move from cell to cell (the row becomes the selection; Shift+↑/↓ extends it), Enter or F2 edits the cell, typing replaces its content, and Tab / Enter save and move on. Esc puts the cursor away. Press ? for every shortcut.
Resize a column by dragging the edge of its header (the left edge for columns right of Task Name, the right edge for the others); double-click the edge to fit it to its content. Right-click a header for Fit to content, Fit all columns, Default width and Reset all column widths (also in the Columns menu). Widths are remembered on this device and shared by the Tasks and Gantt lists; a resized Task Name keeps its width instead of filling the pane.
After an edit the cells it changed are shaded pale yellow (blue is the selection) — a later task that moved, a Finish or Work that was recalculated — as in MS Project. What you typed yourself is not shaded; the next edit, Undo or Redo clears it. Switch it off with Highlight what the last edit changed in the Columns menu.
The list starts with Task Name, Start, Finish, Duration, % Complete, Predecessors, Resource and Status; Task Mode, WBS, the Actual dates, Remaining Duration, Task Type, Work, Cost, the baseline and variance columns and your custom fields start hidden (Columns shows them). The Gantt's list starts with just Name, Start, Finish, Duration and % Complete. Click a Resource or actual-date cell to edit it, or use the task dialog.
Resource takes names separated by commas or semicolons ("Anna, Ben") — typing a new name adds it to the plan's resource pool automatically, the same way MS Project does. Give a share other than full time with Name[NN%] ("Anna[50%], Ben"), as in MS Project — a bare name is 100%. In the list a share other than 100% shows as a small % chip next to the name, so it stays visible however narrow the column is.
The Resources tab lists everyone: type, Max Units (how much of a resource is available: 100% is one full-time person, 300% three people pooled into one; only Work resources have it), rates and cost per use. Renaming or removing someone there updates every task that names them; Days off on a row opens that person's own days off, on top of the plan's working week.
Its Columns button shows or hides columns — Material Label, Ovt Rate and Code start hidden and appear by themselves once a resource uses them. Resize the columns like the task list's: drag a header's edge, double-click it to fit, right-click for more.
The Resource Plan tab shows each person's load as bars with the % written in (of their Max Units), red where they're over capacity — click a red bar to see the tasks behind it and jump to one. Its toolbar has a legend, Level… and Over-allocated only; the people themselves are edited in the Resources tab next to it.
Schedule → Level resources… delays an over-allocated task to the next span with room, never earlier than its own dependencies allow and, by default, never past its own slack (so the plan's finish doesn't move) — turn that off, or scope it to a date on, then Apply. Undo brings it back.
The Resources tab is MS Project's Resource Sheet: Type (Work, Material or Cost), Std/Ovt Rate, Cost per Use, Accrue At and more, editable directly in the grid. A task's Cost column (hidden by default) adds up its assigned resources' rates; a group shows the total of everything in it. The currency is a plan setting: the money columns show it — "Std Rate (€)" — and a click on it opens Plan settings → Currency.
Custom fields
Every task can carry fields of your own — text, numbers, dates and yes/no ticks (up to five of each). Plan settings → Custom fields (also reached from Add field on the task dialog's Custom fields tab, or Manage custom fields… under Columns) creates them: pick a kind, name it, and the In list switch shows it as a column. Fill them in on the task dialog's tab or straight in the list (click a cell; a flag toggles).
In Manage fields you name, rename and remove fields (removing one deletes its values; Undo brings them back). The names are saved with the plan, so another plan can use its own. Custom fields can be filtered like any column and are included in the Excel export.
Filtering
Click the funnel in a column header (every column has one) for an Excel-style filter. Dates get rules — equals, before, after, between, or relative to today such as this week, next month or year to date — and a Year › Month › Day list. Text columns get contains / begins with / ends with / equals and their negatives; numbers get equals, greater or less than, and between.
Every column also has a list of its values to tick, with a search box and (Blanks) for tasks that have no value.
Filters on several columns combine, so a task must match all of them. A group stays visible while any sub-task inside it matches, and stays open while a filter is on.
The bar under the toolbar shows what is filtered and how many tasks are showing; click × on a chip, or Clear all, to remove it. Filters are only for looking — they aren't saved, and a task you add or edit stays visible until you filter again.
The view
Recurring task… (the arrow beside Add Task) makes a meeting or report that repeats — daily, weekly on chosen days, monthly or yearly, a number of times or until a date. It becomes a group of tasks, each pinned to its date; a date on a day off moves to the next working day. Click the ↻ by its name to change the pattern.
In the status bar, Today scrolls the chart to today and Scroll to task to the selected task's bar.
The left side is the same task list as in the Tasks view — the same filters, editing and buttons — with the chart to its right. Drag the thin strip between them to change how much room the list gets. It scrolls sideways when it has more columns than fit, and its ID … Task Name columns stay in place.
Fit (the standard) spreads the whole plan across the chart's width and follows the window; Week / Month / Year are fixed scales — all of them at the right of the status bar, next to the zoom slider (or its − / +), which gives any scale in between. A bar too short for its name has it written beside it, and a milestone's name sits next to it. Year shows quarters; Week is labelled by calendar week (CW — weeks start on Monday, ISO 8601). Days off are shaded.
Working with bars
Drag a bar to reschedule it and drag its edges to resize it. Click a bar or a row to edit it.
Drag the small circle on a bar's right edge onto another task to create a dependency.
The ruler button shows or hides the baseline line under the bars.
Dependency arrows: point the mouse at a bar or milestone (or select its row) and its own links stand out while the others fade — handy in a busy chart. Red arrows are on the critical path.
Progress line (toolbar) draws a purple line from the status date through every task's progress point: it bends left through tasks that are behind and right through those ahead. The status date is today unless you set one in Plan settings → Scheduling rules.
Printing
Print / PDF… (the Data menu, or Ctrl/Cmd+P) lays the list and the chart out on pages of the paper you choose — A4, A3, Letter, Legal or Tabloid, landscape or portrait. The whole timeline is fitted to the page width, long plans continue on the next page with the heading repeated, and a live preview shows every page.
In the Print window, Picture: Copy / PNG / SVG makes the chart as one picture with every row, with the same columns and options — for a slide or a document. SVG keeps the text as text, so PowerPoint, Illustrator or Inkscape can edit it; PNG is 2× sharp; Copy puts the PNG on the clipboard.
Choose the list columns, the time range, the timescale (weeks, months or quarters — automatic by default), and whether to show the baseline, the critical path, dependency arrows, the today line and days off. Tasks print as the list shows them (folded groups and filters apply) unless you expand every group. In your browser's print dialog choose Save as PDF for a file.
Critical path
The route icon in the toolbar highlights the critical path — the chain of tasks with no float left that determines the project's finish. It follows the real schedule and all four link types with their lags and leads, counted in working days. Manual tasks and summary tasks are left out.
Plans
Each plan has its own tasks, its own daily backups and its own linked file, so switching plans also switches which file is kept in sync. Deleting a plan only removes it from this browser; its file is never touched.
Files and sync
Every plan is kept as a plain JSON file in a folder on your disk (choosing the folder is required, in Chrome/Edge). Every change is saved to it automatically, and in an iCloud Drive, OneDrive or Dropbox folder it keeps your own devices in step. New plan and Duplicate ask for the folder; Open plan from folder… opens a plan file that is already there.
Conflicted copies. When two devices save at once, OneDrive or Dropbox keeps one file and renames the other (plan-DESKTOP-4F2.json, plan (1).json, plan_PC.json). Because Milestone sees the whole folder it merges them in — the newer version of each task wins — and renames them merged_…. Nothing is deleted; the merge is listed for review. A plan linked to a single file (from an older version) shows a Link folder reminder next to the file button.
Daily backups. The first time you open a plan or save it each day, Milestone also writes a dated snapshot into a Backups subfolder of its linked folder — one file per day, kept forever. It never overwrites what is already there for the day.
You can disconnect a plan (click the “Linked” button at the top right, or use the plan menu) — the file is kept, and Milestone asks you to choose a folder straight away. Hover the button to see which file the plan is linked to. If the file is moved or deleted, Milestone asks you to pick another file in the same folder or create a new one. Chrome does not allow Desktop, Documents or Downloads themselves as the folder — pick one inside them.
Working together on one file
When several people (or devices) use the same linked file, Milestone reads the file before it writes, so a save never wipes out someone else's work. Changes to different things — even different fields of the same task — are all kept.
If you and someone else changed the same field, the newer edit is kept and an amber conflicts badge appears next to the file name: click it to see both versions and take the other one if it should have won. Tasks that depend on something that moved are re-planned after a merge.
Import, export and backups
Data → Export / Import moves a full JSON snapshot of the current plan out or in.
Export to CSV saves the task list as a plain text table: the columns you choose, dates and durations as the list shows them, sub-tasks indented. Pick the separator your Excel expects (comma or semicolon). Import it again with Import tasks (MS Project XML, CSV)….
Export to Excel saves a formatted .xlsx workbook: a task list plus an optional Gantt chart sheet, each sheet using the columns you chose in its own view.
Import tasks (MS Project XML, CSV)… reads a plan saved from MS Project as XML (File → Save As → XML Format): tasks and their outline, dates, % complete, actual dates, links with lags, manual mode, constraints, resources, baselines, the working week and the holidays. A file with real times of day switches the plan to Hours & minutes scheduling too (when "Import working calendar" is ticked), recovering the working hours and breaks from it.
Export MS Project XML (Data menu) saves the whole plan as a .xml file that MS Project opens: File → Open, file type “XML Format”. Outline, dates, durations, links with lag, constraints, actual dates, baselines, resources, the working week and holidays go along, each task's real time of day included for an hours & minutes plan; empty lines are left out, and custom-field values and TBD dates go into the task’s Notes.
It also reads a CSV with a header row — English or German column names such as Task Name, Start, Finish, Duration, Predecessors, Outline Level. A preview shows what was found; you add the tasks to this plan or replace its tasks (a backup file is downloaded first).
Print / PDF… is under Data as well — see the Gantt chart topic.
Local Backups keeps a rolling daily snapshot of every plan in this browser.
Nothing here ever leaves your machine except into the files you choose.
